author: hannah-grace
title: How to Lament: Naming the Wound You Stopped Naming
dek: How to lament when an old pain has gone quiet: the four movements of Lamentations 3 and a written prayer of lament for this week.
seo_title: How to Lament: Naming the Wound You Stopped Naming
seo_description: How to lament, step by step: the four movements of Lamentations 3 (KJV) and a twenty-minute written prayer of lament for an old wound.
pull_quote: Your wound doesn't have to be the worst wound in the room to deserve a name.
body_html:
Some wounds don't bleed. They just settle in.

They live somewhere below the ribs, quiet and heavy, and after enough years you almost stop noticing them. You still bring the casserole and bow your head during the slow songs. From the outside, you look fine.

But at night, when the house is finally still, something you have no name for sits down beside you.

If that is you, you have not failed at faith. You were never shown how to lament.

Lament is honest speech to God about what hurts. The Bible is full of it, and one short passage in Lamentations shows its whole shape. Below is that passage, then a prayer of lament you can write this week in about twenty minutes.

Bandages too small for the wound

"Just trust God." "Count it all joy" (James 1:2, KJV). We reach for words like these the moment the ache surfaces. The words are true. They are being pressed against a wound that hasn't been cleaned yet.

Somewhere along the way, many of us decided that admitting we still hurt, especially about something old, was an accusation against God's faithfulness. So we performed healed. We mistook silence for healing, and performance for peace.

What the poet does first

Lamentations is a book of grief over the fall of Jerusalem. The city had been burned and its people carried into exile. In the middle of that grief, the poet writes:

"Remembering mine affliction and my misery, the wormwood and the gall. My soul hath them still in remembrance, and is humbled in me. This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." (Lamentations 3:19-23, KJV)

Read it slowly and notice the order. Before "great is thy faithfulness," he names it all: affliction, misery, wormwood, gall. His soul is humbled in him, and he says so. Hope appears only after the naming.

How to lament in four movements

That is the shape of lament, in four movements. Each has its own line in the passage.

  • Remember. "Remembering mine affliction and my misery." Let the wound be real, without minimizing it.
  • Acknowledge. "...and is humbled in me." Name what it has done to you on the inside.
  • Hope. "This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope." Hope here is something he calls back to mind on purpose, before he feels it.
  • Choose. "Great is thy faithfulness." He says one true thing about who God is while the rubble is still around him.

Picture a woman I'll call Carolyn. She is a composite, drawn from what many women describe. She sits with her pen over a blank page for ten minutes, thinking: my thing isn't bad enough. Other women have it so much worse. Who am I to lament? Then she writes the sentence she has never said out loud, that her marriage has felt empty for four years. Nothing dramatic by anyone else's scale, and it has been sitting below her ribs all that time. Your wound doesn't have to be the worst wound in the room to deserve a name.

Your wound doesn't have to be the worst wound in the room to deserve a name.

Even Jesus, standing at the tomb of His friend Lazarus and knowing what He was about to do, did not hurry past the grief. "Jesus wept." (John 11:35, KJV) Grief and faith can live in the same heart. You do not have to be okay before you come to God with your wound. You just have to come.

A prayer of lament to write this week

This is the written lament from Chapter 1 of the book. Give yourself at least twenty minutes without interruption, a pen and a page. Prayer requests and gratitude lists can wait for another day. This is honest speech, addressed directly to God, about what you are carrying right now. Work through each movement in order. There is no right way to do it.

  1. Pause for sixty seconds. Place your hand on your chest and ask God one question: What am I not saying? Notice what surfaces.
  2. Remember. Begin with "I remember..." Describe the wound, the loss, the betrayal or the grief. Name it as specifically as you can. What happened? What did it cost you?
  3. Acknowledge. Begin with "And my soul is humbled in me because..." Write how it has settled inside you. What do you feel, and where do you feel it? What have you stopped believing because of it?
  4. Let it stand. Read what you wrote once, and leave it as it is. If you feel the pull to add "but I'm grateful for..." right away, wait.
  5. Hope. Begin with "This I recall to my mind..." You are not required to feel hopeful when you write this. Write what you know to be true about God, even now. It can be small, just one thing.
  6. Choose. Begin with "Today I choose to believe..." Declare one specific truth about God's character, and leave your circumstances out of the sentence.

A fear often comes up here: if I open this door, the grief will sweep me away. Naming is a smaller act than that. You are giving the wound a word or a sentence.

And if the page stays blank, or twenty minutes is more than today allows, write one sentence and stop: "Lord, I am carrying ______, and I have been carrying it since ______, and I have been afraid to bring it to You because ______."

That is the beginning of a lament. And it is holy ground.

The book takes this lament further. Chapter 1 of Healing Bible Study for Women adds a second exercise for finding the true name of what you have been calling stress or a hard season, five reflection questions and a closing prayer written in full. Five more chapters follow, one for each week.

What you might notice

Tears, sometimes. The kind that have been waiting a long time. You can let them come, and you can set the pen down until they pass.

You might feel lighter afterward, or simply tired. You might also notice nothing. The words may look flat on the page, and the third movement may not come at all. Scripture has room for that. Psalm 88 is a prayer that never arrives at praise. Its last line is "and mine acquaintance into darkness" (Psalm 88:18, KJV), and it was kept in the Bible just as it stands. If hope will not come today, stop after the second movement and return another day. An unfinished lament is still a prayer.

Writing a lament is no guarantee that the wound will close, and a wound that stays open says nothing about the size of your faith. If the pain is deep, or has been with you for a long time, it can also deserve the help of a pastor, a counselor or a doctor. Asking for that help is one more way of naming it.

When to use it

  • When the numbness settles in. Do only the first step: sixty seconds, a hand on your chest, one question.
  • When you hear yourself say "I'm good, just busy." Take the full twenty minutes that evening, with all four movements.
  • When an old grief comes back. The book calls this pattern a rhythm. Women return to it again and again, sometimes for the same wound at a different depth.

If you would like a structure to keep going, here is how to begin a Bible study for women who are hurting.

Questions women ask about how to lament

What is a prayer of lament? A prayer of lament is honest speech to God about what hurts. Lamentations 3:19-23 shows its shape in four movements: remember, acknowledge, hope and choose. The naming comes first, and hope appears only after it.

How do you write a lament? Give yourself at least twenty minutes, a pen and a page, and address God directly. Begin with "I remember..." and work through the four movements in order. If that is more than today allows, write one sentence about what you are carrying and stop.

Is lament a lack of faith? No. The poet of Lamentations names his affliction and his misery before he says a word about God's faithfulness, and Jesus did not hurry past the grief at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35). Grief and faith can live in the same heart.

When prayer itself has gone quiet and you are tired of asking, The God Who Heals at Bitter Water is the next reflection to sit with.

And on the ordinary days, when the trouble is a blank page more than an old wound, these prayer journal ideas give you a first line to borrow.

The book is a six-week Bible study for women, and this lament is where it begins. Its pages give you lined space for each movement.

This reflection comes from Chapter 1 of Healing Bible Study for Women by Hannah Grace. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.

author: hannah-grace
title: Healing Scriptures for the Woman Tired of Asking: Bitter Water
dek: Healing scriptures for the long wait: the God who heals at bitter water, the woman who reached anyway, and a prayer for flat days.
seo_title: Healing Scriptures for the Woman Tired of Asking
seo_description: Healing scriptures for women tired of asking: Exodus 15, Mark 5, six KJV verses to write out or pray, and a 15 to 20 minute practice.
pull_quote: Healing is not a reward for having finished suffering. It is a name God wears into the middle of it.
body_html:
Three days after the Red Sea, the singing stopped.

If you have gone looking for healing scriptures after a long stretch of asking, begin here, with people who had run out of water and patience at the same time. Israel had just watched God part the sea. Miriam had led the women out with timbrels and dancing. Then they walked three days into the wilderness, found water at last, and could not drink it. It was bitter, and the place was named for it: Marah, which means bitter.

The people murmured against Moses. Moses cried to the LORD, the LORD showed him a tree, and when he cast it into the water, the water was made sweet. There, beside that water, God gives Himself a name:

"For I am the LORD that healeth thee." (Exodus 15:26, KJV)

The God Who Heals at Bitter Water

He speaks this name at Marah itself, to people who were murmuring a few verses earlier and who still have a wilderness to cross.

Healing is not a reward for having finished suffering. It is a name God wears into the middle of it.

Healing is not a reward for having finished suffering. It is a name God wears into the middle of it.

If you have prayed for healing for a long time, you may know a quieter ache: the embarrassment of asking again. Picture a woman I'll call Denise. She is a composite, her story gathered from many women's. She has prayed about the same body for three years, and lately she feels she is bothering God, as if repeating one request this many times must mean she is doing something wrong.

It is easy to read healing promises like a vending machine: insert enough faith, receive the outcome. When the outcome doesn't come, we blame our faith. That reading makes God smaller and the suffering larger. A body that has not healed is no verdict on your faith.

Asking God does not compete with seeing your doctor, either. Prayer goes alongside medical care and does not replace it. Keep your appointments, keep taking what you have been prescribed, and pray as you go.

The woman who reached anyway

Mark tells of a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years, and she had tried everything. She "had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse." (Mark 5:26, KJV)

Mark names the physicians to show how long and how costly her asking had been, with no reproach for having gone to them.

She didn't push to the front. She came up in the crowd behind Jesus and "touched his garment" (Mark 5:27, KJV). Matthew remembers that it was "the hem of his garment" (Matthew 9:20, KJV).

Jesus stopped and looked for her. She came forward "fearing and trembling," and she "told him all the truth" (Mark 5:33, KJV). He answered: "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague." (Mark 5:34, KJV)

Daughter. She expected to be exposed, and she was given a family name.

Her faith that day looked like a hand going out through a crowd after twelve years of nothing working. Mark gives us her story as hers, and it sets no schedule for yours. Some women reach for years and are still sick, and their reaching is no smaller than hers. Some days, the prayer is just the reaching.

Five more healing scriptures to write out or pray

Exodus 15:26 is the first. Chapter 3 of the book builds a seven-day prayer on it and on passages like these. Think of them as healing scriptures for women who are tired of asking: words to copy onto a card or pray slowly. None of them is a formula, and none comes with a date.

  • Psalm 103:2-3. "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits: Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases" (KJV) The hard word is "all." Many illnesses are not healed in this life, and you may know that in your own body. You can pray this verse and say so in the same breath.
  • Psalm 147:3. "He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds." (KJV) For the hurt no scan will show.
  • Jeremiah 17:14. "Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved: for thou art my praise." (KJV) A prayer to borrow whole when you have no words of your own.
  • 2 Corinthians 12:9. "And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." (KJV) Paul had asked three times for his thorn to be taken away, and it stayed. For whatever has stayed with you.
  • 1 Peter 2:24. "Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed." (KJV) Peter is writing about the cross and about sin. Pray it as thanks for what is already finished.

If you want to keep copying verses by hand, the 2027 scripture writing plan sets aside October for eight passages on healing and comfort.

A practice for the flat days

In the book, this is the step for the week when prayer feels like it is landing on a ceiling. Instead of stopping, you tell God about the silence. Set aside 15 to 20 minutes, the time the book gives each day of its seven-day prayer, and bring your Bible, a journal and a pen.

  1. Name what you are bringing. Write one specific sentence. Skip the category ("my health") and write the particular thing, such as the pain that wakes you at 3 a.m. or the diagnosis you are tired of explaining.
  2. Name the absence out loud. Say: "Lord, I don't feel You in this right now. I'm naming that honestly. I'm choosing to stay at Marah anyway." If you are tired of asking, or embarrassed to ask again, tell Him that too.
  3. Read Exodus 15:26 slowly, once. Read it aloud if you can.
  4. Write what comes. Answer one question in a sentence or two: "Lord, where have You been healing me that I haven't acknowledged?" If nothing comes, write that. As the book puts it, the blank page in front of God is still a prayer.
  5. Copy one verse by hand. Choose the verse that landed hardest and write it out word for word. Under it, add one sentence about why it hit you.

If the hurt underneath has never been said out loud at all, begin with The Wound You Stopped Naming, a short way into lament from Lamentations 3.

This page holds one sitting. Chapter 3 of Healing Bible Study for Women lays out the whole seven-day prayer, with one passage and one written prompt for each day, and adds writing exercises with lined space for your answers, the week's reflection questions and a closing prayer.

What you might notice, and when to use it

The book asks you to watch for what shifts in your posture toward the trouble while the trouble itself stays the same. You may feel a little less embarrassed about asking. You may cry. You may notice nothing at all, and nothing is an honest result that needs no fixing.

This practice does not make a body well, and you cannot fail it. If it stirs up more than you can carry alone, stop and tell someone you trust. James tells the church to "pray one for another" (James 5:16, KJV).

  • The night before an appointment or a test result, alongside whatever your doctor has asked you to do.
  • The morning you catch yourself skipping prayer because you have asked so many times already.
  • Once a day for a week, with a different scripture from this page each day.

Questions women ask about healing scriptures

Where does the Bible call God a healer? In Exodus 15:26, beside the bitter water of Marah, God names Himself the LORD who heals. He speaks that name to people who were murmuring a few verses earlier and who still had a wilderness to cross.

Is it wrong to keep asking God for healing? No. The woman in Mark 5 had been ill for twelve years, and her faith that day looked like a hand going out through a crowd. If you are tired of asking, or embarrassed to ask again, you can tell Him that too.

Does it mean my faith is weak if I have not been healed? No. A body that has not healed is no verdict on your faith. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be taken away, and it stayed.

The singing had stopped at Marah, and God spoke there anyway.

This reflection comes from Chapter 3 of Healing Bible Study for Women by Hannah Grace. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.

title: December Scripture Writing Plan: Peace for an Anxious Heart (KJV)
dek: A December scripture writing plan from the KJV: eight passages on peace, two a week, with rest days and one ten-minute practice.
seo_title: December Scripture Writing Plan: Peace Verses (KJV)
seo_description: A December scripture writing plan (KJV): eight peace passages in four weeks, how to write, reflect and remember, and one ten-minute practice.
pull_quote: You cannot skim a sentence you are writing by hand.
body_html:
It is the first week of December, and the kitchen table already holds a stack of cards, a school form and a list that grew overnight. The house is still dark. You have ten minutes before anyone else is awake, and your mind has already left for the twentieth.

A scripture writing plan is made for those ten minutes. It asks one thing of you: copy a short passage of the Bible by hand, slowly, and stay with it for a few days. This December scripture writing plan uses eight passages about peace from the King James Version, two a week, with rest days built in.

Begin with what it cannot do. Writing a verse will not finish the list or lighten a hard month, and nobody can promise that it will quiet an anxious heart. What it gives you is smaller and still worth having: one true sentence, and ten minutes in which your hand and your attention are in the same place.

How a scripture writing plan works: write, reflect, remember

Copying Scripture is an old habit. In Deuteronomy, the king of Israel was told to write out his own copy of the law and read it all the days of his life (Deuteronomy 17:18-19). The psalmist says why in one line: "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee." (Psalm 119:11, KJV)

Writing by hand slows you down. Your hand has to follow every word, including the small ones you have read past for years. You cannot skim a sentence you are writing by hand.

You cannot skim a sentence you are writing by hand.

The journal this plan comes from gives every passage two pages, one to write it out and one to reflect. On some of the reflection pages you write the passage again from memory. For December, I have spread that work across three short days:

  • Write. Copy the passage word for word, thee and thou included.
  • Reflect. Read your copy and answer one question about it in a few honest sentences.
  • Remember. Write it again from memory. Peek if you need to. Memory grows by trying.

The December plan: eight passages, four weeks

This part of the journal has eight passages, so the plan has eight, in the same order. I have not added verses to fill thirty-one days. Each passage gets three days, every seventh day is rest, and the last three days of the month are for looking back. The list gives the first words of each passage. Copy the whole verse from your Bible.

Week 1: John 14:27 and Isaiah 26:3

  • December 1: Write John 14:27. "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you..." (KJV)
  • December 2: Reflect on John 14:27.
  • December 3: Remember. Write John 14:27 again from memory.
  • December 4: Write Isaiah 26:3. "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace..." (KJV)
  • December 5: Reflect on Isaiah 26:3.
  • December 6: Remember. Write Isaiah 26:3 again from memory.
  • December 7: Rest.

Week 2: 1 Peter 5:7 and Psalm 94:19

  • December 8: Write 1 Peter 5:7. "Casting all your care upon him..." (KJV)
  • December 9: Reflect on 1 Peter 5:7.
  • December 10: Remember. Write 1 Peter 5:7 again from memory.
  • December 11: Write Psalm 94:19. "In the multitude of my thoughts within me..." (KJV)
  • December 12: Reflect on Psalm 94:19.
  • December 13: Remember. Write Psalm 94:19 again from memory.
  • December 14: Rest.

Week 3: Matthew 6:34 and Psalm 56:3

  • December 15: Write Matthew 6:34. "Take therefore no thought for the morrow..." (KJV)
  • December 16: Reflect on Matthew 6:34.
  • December 17: Remember. Write Matthew 6:34 again from memory.
  • December 18: Write Psalm 56:3. "What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee." (KJV)
  • December 19: Reflect on Psalm 56:3.
  • December 20: Remember. Write Psalm 56:3 again from memory.
  • December 21: Rest.

Week 4: 2 Thessalonians 3:16 and Psalm 55:22

  • December 22: Write 2 Thessalonians 3:16. "Now the Lord of peace himself give you peace always by all means..." (KJV)
  • December 23: Reflect on 2 Thessalonians 3:16.
  • December 24: Remember. Write 2 Thessalonians 3:16 again from memory.
  • December 25: Write Psalm 55:22. "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee..." (KJV)
  • December 26: Reflect on Psalm 55:22.
  • December 27: Remember. Write Psalm 55:22 again from memory.
  • December 28: Rest.

The last three days: looking back

  • December 29: Look back over the eight passages.
  • December 30: Choose the one passage you want to keep.
  • December 31: Write it once more.

The dates are a guide. Start late if you need to, and keep the order. If you miss a day, skip it and keep going, because nothing resets. On a day with only five minutes, just write the verse. The reflection can wait.

The third week holds the one creative practice in this part of the journal, a breath prayer on Psalm 56:3. Breathe at your ordinary pace, with no holding and no counting, and stop if it feels uncomfortable. Say the first half of the verse as you breathe in, "What time I am afraid," and the second half as you breathe out, "I will trust in thee." (Psalm 56:3, KJV) Then write two short lists: what you are afraid of today, and what you will trust Him with.

One day, start to finish

Here is December 1 in full. Every "write" day follows the same shape. You need a King James Bible, a pen, and a notebook or a plain index card. Give it about ten minutes. The journal sets no timer.

The passage: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid." (John 14:27, KJV)

  1. Sit down before you open anything else. Phone face down, in another room if you can.
  2. Read the passage aloud once. Go slowly enough to hear the pause in the middle.
  3. Copy it word for word. Keep the old verb endings and the punctuation.
  4. Underline the word or phrase that stopped you. Choose one. It might be "my peace." It might be "afraid."
  5. Read your own handwriting back. Once, silently, as if someone had left it on the table for you.
  6. Close with one sentence of thanks. A small one counts. Then shut the notebook.

On December 2, the reflect day, open to your copy and answer the question the journal asks of this verse: how is the peace Jesus gives different from the peace the world offers me? For the other passages, two plain questions will serve. What does this show me about God? Where do I need this right now? On December 3, turn to a clean page and write the verse from memory.

In Scripture Journal for Women, each of these eight passages is printed at the top of a lined page, followed by a reflection page with a question written for that passage. The breath prayer on Psalm 56:3 has a practice page of its own, and the part closes with a Looking Back page.

What you might notice

You might notice a word you have read past for years. You might notice nothing. Nothing is an honest result, and the verse is on the page either way.

Some of these passages touch fear and weariness, and December can press on both. If writing stirs up more than you can carry, put the pen down, drink a glass of water and talk to someone you trust. If anxiety is with you most days, it deserves the help of a doctor or a counselor as well as your prayers. Asking for that help is no failure of faith.

If what surfaces is an old grief more than a present worry, you may need different words first. How to lament walks through the four movements of Lamentations 3. If this is a December of waiting on a body, there are healing scriptures for the woman tired of asking that you can write out the same way.

When to use this scripture writing plan

  • Early mornings. Before the phone, while the house is dark.
  • Advent. If you keep Advent, the four weeks sit beside it easily. The plan reaches Christmas Eve with "Now the Lord of peace himself give you peace always by all means. The Lord be with you all." (2 Thessalonians 3:16, KJV)
  • A hard December. The first one after a loss, a month of money worry, a week of waiting on test results. Two passages a week is small enough to keep when little else is.

New to this? Scripture writing for beginners walks through a first session, one verse at a time.

Questions women ask about a scripture writing plan

What is a scripture writing plan? It is a list of short Bible passages to copy by hand, slowly, on set days. This one has eight passages about peace from the King James Version, two a week through December, with rest days built in.

How do I start scripture writing? For this plan you need a King James Bible, a pen, and a notebook or a plain index card. Read the passage aloud once, copy it word for word, and underline the word or phrase that stopped you. About ten minutes is enough.

How many verses should I write a day? One passage. In this plan the same passage stays with you for three days, to write, reflect and remember. On a day with only five minutes, just write the verse.

The journal holds 96 passages in twelve parts, and these eight make up one part. A notebook will do the same work this month.

When December ends, the 2027 scripture writing plan sets all twelve parts across the year, one theme a month.

The list on the kitchen table will still be there when the ten minutes are over. So will the verse, in your own handwriting.

This plan follows Part 3 of Scripture Journal for Women by Hannah Grace. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.

title: Prayer Journal Ideas: How to Begin When You Don't Know What to Say
dek: Prayer journal ideas for the blank page: how one week of a guided journal works, six pages to try, and a ten-minute practice for today.
seo_title: Prayer Journal Ideas: How to Begin a Prayer Journal
seo_description: Prayer journal ideas when you don't know what to say: six prompts with KJV verses and a ten-minute, four-line practice to start today.
pull_quote: One honest word on the page is already a prayer.
body_html:
The notebook is open on the kitchen table. The coffee beside it is going cold. You wrote the date at the top of the page ten minutes ago, and you have written nothing since.

If you went looking for prayer journal ideas because you love the thought of writing your prayers and have no notion what belongs on the first line, you are in good company. The journal these ideas come from says it plainly: "Most of us were never taught how to pray."

Below is how one week of that journal is laid out, six ideas from its pages, and a ten-minute practice you can do today on any sheet of paper.

How to start a prayer journal: borrow a shape

A blank page asks you to invent a prayer from nothing. A shape gives you a first line. In Daily Prayer Journal for Women, every week has four pages:

  • The week opener. A verse from the King James Version, a short reflection, a prayer to begin, and a practice that grows out of that week's verse.
  • Days 1 to 3 and Days 4 to 6. Three short daily entries per page. You write the date and fill in as much as you want.
  • Day 7, Looking Back. Two reflection questions written for that week's verse, plus space for answered prayers and what you are carrying forward.

The journal runs fifty-two weeks, in four parts of thirteen weeks each, and it is undated. In the first part, Coming Near, every daily entry has the same four lines: "Lord, I praise You for," "What I'm laying down today," "What I'm asking You for," and "Thank You for." In the book's words, that order "keeps prayer from becoming only a list of requests."

Six prayer journal ideas from the first thirteen weeks

Each week's practice is different. These six come from Part One, and each works with a pen and a plain page. Use them as prayer journal prompts on the days your own words run out.

  • Pour it out (Week 2). The verse is "Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah." (Psalm 62:8, KJV) The page shows a pitcher and gives one instruction: "Write everything in your heart inside the pitcher. Messy is fine." Draw any container, fill it with words, then finish the sentence underneath: "You are my refuge because..."
  • Praise from A to Z (Week 4). "Name who God is or something He has done, one letter at a time." The book suggests coming back to the list on a hard day.
  • Three doors (Week 7). Jesus says, "Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you" (Matthew 7:7, KJV). The page draws three doors and asks for one honest request behind each. Ask: what I need. Seek: what I'm looking for. Knock: what I won't give up on. Nothing on the page says when a door opens.
  • Line by line (Week 9). Copy the Lord's Prayer one line at a time, beginning with "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name" (Matthew 6:9, KJV). The instruction: "Pray one line, then write your own words under it."
  • Pray without words (Week 11). "Write a name or a single word in the center. Then let your pen move around it while you pray: lines, dots, waves." The week rests on this verse: "Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered." (Romans 8:26, KJV)
  • Morning and evening (Week 12). Make two columns. Under "Before the phone," write one sentence to God each morning. Under "Where I saw Him," write one moment each evening.

If the request behind your third door is for a body that has not healed, and you have knocked for a long time, these healing scriptures for the woman tired of asking were gathered for that wait.

And if copying the Lord's Prayer line by line suits you, the December scripture writing plan gives you eight passages on peace to write out the same way.

When you still don't know what to say

Picture a woman I'll call Ruth. She is a composite, drawn from what many women describe. She has three journals in a drawer. Each one holds four or five careful entries and then blank pages, because she believed every prayer had to sound like the ones she hears at church. On the days when you open the journal and stare at the lines, the book's instruction is to "write one word, or a name, or simply 'Help.'" One honest word on the page is already a prayer.

One honest word on the page is already a prayer.

A ten-minute practice for today

This is the daily entry from the journal's first part, moved onto any sheet of paper. The book sets no length of time for it. Ten minutes is enough, and five will do. You need a pen and Psalm 62:8, which is printed above.

  1. Write today's date at the top of the page.
  2. Read Psalm 62:8 slowly, one phrase at a time. The book calls this praying the verse: you turn a phrase into a sentence to God. "Pour out your heart" might become "Lord, here is what is in my heart this morning."
  3. Write "Lord, I praise You for" and finish it in one line. Begin with who God is.
  4. Write "What I'm laying down today" and give it two lines. Name the weight as specifically as you can: the appointment on Thursday, the text you have not answered.
  5. Write "What I'm asking You for" and give it two lines. Ask plainly.
  6. Write "Thank You for" and finish it in one line. As the book says of gratitude, a warm cup of coffee counts.
  7. Stop. Leave the page as it is, crossed-out words and all.

In Daily Prayer Journal for Women these lines are already printed, three entries to a page, so all you bring is the date and a pen. Each week opens with its own verse, reflection and prayer and closes with a Day 7 page for looking back, and there are pages for the names you are carrying in prayer.

What you might notice

You might notice that the laying-down lines fill fastest. You might also notice nothing. The page may read like a grocery list, and you may feel exactly as you did before you sat down. That is an honest result. It says nothing about the size of your faith, and it is no sign that you went unheard.

Sometimes the two lines turn out to be too small. If an old hurt surfaces there, it may need a longer prayer, and how to lament walks through one. The journal's own advice after a heavy page is simple: stand up, stretch, drink a glass of water. If the heaviness has not lifted by the end of the day, set the page aside and talk to someone you trust, such as a friend, your pastor or a counselor.

When to use it

  • Before the phone. The first minutes of the morning, while the coffee is still hot.
  • In the parked car. The book counts a parked car or a laundry room as a fine place to pray.
  • At night, when the names of people you promised to pray for keep circling. Write the names only. That is the whole entry.

If you miss a day, the book's rule is five words long: "Skip it and keep going."

For the weeks when even these feel like too much, there are prayer journal prompts for when life is heavy.

Questions women ask about prayer journal ideas

What is a prayer journal? A prayer journal is a notebook where you write your prayers down. A blank page asks you to invent each prayer from nothing. A guided journal gives the page a shape, so a first line is already in front of you.

What do you write in a prayer journal? Four lines are enough: "Lord, I praise You for," "What I'm laying down today," "What I'm asking You for," and "Thank You for." On the days your own words run out, try one of the six ideas above, such as praise from A to Z or the Lord's Prayer copied one line at a time.

How do I start a prayer journal when I don't know what to say? Write today's date, then one word, or a name, or simply "Help." One honest word on the page is already a prayer. If you miss a day, skip it and keep going.

In the paperback each of these practices is drawn on its week's opening page, and the journal carries on for a full year. After the first thirteen weeks the four daily lines change with each part: When Life Is Heavy, Praying for the People I Love, and Growing in Trust.

The coffee will likely go cold again tomorrow. The page under your hand will have something on it.

These ideas come from Daily Prayer Journal for Women by Hannah Grace. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.

author: hannah-grace
title: 2027 Scripture Writing Plan: Twelve Themes for Twelve Months (KJV)
dek: A 2027 scripture writing plan: one theme a month, eight KJV passages each, and a fifteen-minute way to write, reflect and remember.
seo_title: Scripture Writing Plan 2027: Twelve Monthly Themes (KJV)
seo_description: Scripture writing plan 2027: twelve monthly themes, 96 KJV references, two passages a week, and one sitting explained step by step.
pull_quote: A verse copied by hand is a verse read at the speed of your pen.
body_html:
It is the last week of December. The new calendar is still in its wrapper, the tree is dropping needles on the rug, and you have told yourself, again, that this will be the year you stay in the Word.

You remember how far the last reading plan got. Somewhere in February it went quiet, and by spring the bookmark hadn't moved.

This plan for 2027 asks for less, and it gives your hands something to do. One theme a month. Eight short passages. A pen. Below are all twelve months with their references, and one way to sit down with a single passage and write it.

Why write a verse by hand

Copying is slower than reading, and the slowness is the point. Your hand has to follow every word, including the small ones your eyes have skipped for years. A verse copied by hand is a verse read at the speed of your pen.

A verse copied by hand is a verse read at the speed of your pen.

The habit is old. In Deuteronomy 17:18-19, each king of Israel is told to write out his own copy of the law and read it all the days of his life. A psalmist describes where that kind of attention leads: "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee." (Psalm 119:11, KJV)

Every passage in this plan is from the King James Version. Its language is old, and that can help. When you have to slow down for thee and thou, you slow down enough to hear.

How scripture writing works: write, reflect, remember

The journal this plan comes from gives each passage two pages. On the first you write it out, word for word. The second is a reflection page, and those rotate between three kinds: looking closer at the words, making the passage personal, and writing it again from memory. The sitting below borrows one move from each, so you can do it tonight on any lined page.

What you need: a pen, a notebook, and the passage open in a King James Bible. How long: about fifteen minutes. If you only have five, do the first two steps and stop.

Take the last passage in January's list as an example: "The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him." (Nahum 1:7, KJV)

  1. Read it out loud once. Hear the whole sentence before you write any of it.
  2. Copy it word for word. Go slowly. Keep the punctuation, the capitals and the old words exactly as printed.
  3. Underline the phrase that stopped you. One phrase only. In Nahum 1:7 it might be "a strong hold," or "he knoweth."
  4. Answer one question in three lines. Choose either "What does this show me about God?" or "Where do I need this right now?"
  5. Pray it back. Write the verse as a prayer in your own words. One or two sentences are plenty.
  6. Write it again from memory. Cover the passage and try. Peek if you need to. Memory grows by trying.

Scripture Journal for Women prints all 96 passages, each at the top of a lined page, so there is nothing to look up. Its reflection pages take turns among three kinds, Look Closer, Make It Personal and Hide It in My Heart, and every part ends with a Looking Back page.

The 2027 scripture writing plan, month by month

Each month takes one of the twelve parts of the journal, with that part's eight passages in the order the book prints them. The journal has no dates and its parts run in a different order. I matched them to the months of 2027, and each line says why.

  • January: Who God Is. Exodus 34:6; Psalm 23:1-3; Psalm 90:2; Isaiah 40:28; Psalm 103:8; Malachi 3:6; 1 John 4:16; Nahum 1:7. A year in the Word begins with who He says He is.
  • February: Loved and Chosen. Psalm 139:13-14; Jeremiah 31:3; Isaiah 43:1; Ephesians 2:10; 1 Peter 2:9; Zephaniah 3:17; John 15:16; Romans 8:38-39. A fair month to write out a love that lasts.
  • March: Forgiveness and Grace. Ephesians 2:8-9; Psalm 103:12; Isaiah 1:18; Micah 7:19; Ephesians 1:7; 2 Corinthians 5:17; Psalm 32:1; Titus 3:5. Easter falls on March 28 in 2027, and these eight lead up to it.
  • April: Courage and Hope. Psalm 27:1; 2 Timothy 1:7; Psalm 31:24; Jeremiah 29:11; Romans 8:28; Isaiah 43:19; Hebrews 6:19; Psalm 27:14. Spring, and a passage about a new thing.
  • May: Love in Action. 1 Corinthians 13:4-5; 1 Corinthians 13:6-7; John 13:34-35; 1 John 4:19; Romans 12:10; Galatians 5:22-23; 1 Peter 4:8; 1 John 3:18. Mother's Day month, when names and faces are already on your mind.
  • June: Wisdom for Everyday Life. Proverbs 2:6; Proverbs 4:23; Proverbs 16:3; Proverbs 15:1; Proverbs 31:25-26; Proverbs 16:9; Proverbs 19:21; Proverbs 9:10. All eight are from Proverbs, short enough for a porch or a suitcase.
  • July: Faith and Trust. Hebrews 11:1; Psalm 37:5; Psalm 9:10; Mark 9:24; Isaiah 26:4; Psalm 20:7; 2 Corinthians 5:7; Hebrews 11:6. The middle of the year, when January's resolve has thinned.
  • August: Strength for Weary Days. Isaiah 40:29; 2 Corinthians 12:9; Psalm 73:26; Philippians 4:13; Psalm 28:7; Habakkuk 3:19; Galatians 6:9; Psalm 121:1-2. For the end of summer, when the schedule starts to stack up again.
  • September: Peace for an Anxious Heart. John 14:27; Isaiah 26:3; 1 Peter 5:7; Psalm 94:19; Matthew 6:34; Psalm 56:3; 2 Thessalonians 3:16; Psalm 55:22. Fall calendars fill fast.
  • October: Healing and Comfort. Psalm 147:3; Jeremiah 17:14; Isaiah 53:5; Matthew 5:4; Psalm 30:5; Psalm 30:11; Psalm 119:50; Isaiah 43:2. Shorter days, and room for the tender passages before the holidays arrive.
  • November: Gratitude and Praise. Psalm 100:4-5; Psalm 118:24; Psalm 107:1; Psalm 103:1-2; Psalm 9:1; Psalm 150:6; Colossians 3:17; Psalm 63:3. Thanksgiving month. Seven of the eight are psalms.
  • December: Walking with Jesus. John 8:12; John 10:10; John 15:5; Matthew 5:14-16; Luke 10:41-42; John 11:25; Matthew 28:20; John 6:35. The year closes with words Jesus spoke, beginning with the light of the world.

October is the tender month. Its part includes a short written lament, and if lament is new to you, how to lament in four movements shows the shape of one. If you want to stay longer with those passages, there are more healing scriptures for the woman tired of asking. Go gently there. When a verse opens something painful, you can copy it and leave the reflection for another day.

September's eight passages on peace are also paced across four weeks, with rest days, in the December scripture writing plan, if you would rather begin before the new year.

How to pace a month

The arithmetic is simple. Eight passages a month. Two passages a week. Pick two days and keep them: Monday and Thursday, or Saturday morning and Sunday afternoon. Four weeks covers all eight.

February 2027 is exactly four weeks long. Every other month leaves two or three spare days. Use them to rewrite the passage you most want to keep, or to look back over the month and note what changed in how you see God.

Two passages in one sitting on a Sunday counts. So does one passage copied in five minutes, with the reflection left blank.

What you might notice

Sometimes a word stands up that you have read past a hundred times. Sometimes a verse you copied on Monday comes back to you on Wednesday at the sink.

And sometimes, nothing. The page is filled, the handwriting is yours, and you feel exactly as you did before you sat down. That sitting still happened. You read a passage slowly and all the way through, which is more than a hurried morning usually allows. Write the next one on its day. If a passage stirs up more than you can carry today, write only its reference, close the journal and come back to it another day.

When to use it

  • Starting in January. Begin with Exodus 34:6 in the first week and write two passages a week from there.
  • Starting late. Start in any month. If you find this plan in April, open April's list and begin with its first passage. The earlier months will keep.
  • After a missed month. Skip it and keep going with the month you are in. Nothing to catch up, nothing to make up, and no one is keeping count.

New to this? Scripture writing for beginners walks through a first session, one verse at a time.

Questions women ask about a scripture writing plan for 2027

How long does it take to write out a passage? About fifteen minutes for one passage, with all six steps. If you only have five, do the first two steps and stop.

How many verses do I write in a week? Two passages a week, on two days you pick and keep. Four weeks covers the month's eight, and the spare days are for rewriting the passage you most want to keep.

Do I have to start a scripture writing plan in January? No. Start in any month, with the first passage on that month's list. If you miss a month, skip it and keep going with the month you are in.

The book follows the same twelve parts. Each part also has one practice page of its own, and there is a tracker with 96 squares to shade.

This plan follows the twelve parts of Scripture Journal for Women by Hannah Grace. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.

author: hannah-grace
title: Bible Study for Women: How to Begin When You're Hurting
dek: A Bible study for women who are hurting: how one week of a six-week study works, and a twenty-minute first session in John 11.
seo_title: Bible Study for Women: How to Begin When You're Hurting
seo_description: Bible study for women, for beginners: how to start with a Bible and a notebook, read, reflect, respond, and a first session on John 11 (KJV).
pull_quote: Mary did not tidy her grief before she brought it to Jesus.
body_html:
The Bible has been on the nightstand for weeks. You meant to open it. Then the hard thing happened, or kept happening, and now even the thought of a reading plan feels like one more place to fall behind.

If you are looking for a Bible study for women because something hurts and you don't know where to begin, begin smaller than you think. You need a Bible, a notebook and about twenty minutes. You do not need to know where Leviticus is, and you do not need to feel better first.

Below is how one week of a six-week study works, and a complete first session you can do today in John 11.

What a Bible study for women is, and what it isn't

A Bible study is slow reading with a pen in your hand. You read a passage, notice what it actually says, and answer it honestly. A devotional usually hands you a verse and a finished thought. In a study, you do part of the work.

For a woman who is hurting, that matters. A finished thought can feel like a bandage pressed on too fast. A passage read slowly, with room for your own question, meets you where you actually are. It will not fix the hard thing. It gives you a place to bring it.

How to start a Bible study: one week of read, reflect, respond

The session below comes from Healing Bible Study for Women, a six-week study in which each chapter is one week. The book doesn't use the words read, reflect and respond, but every week moves through those three, in roughly this order:

  • Read. The week opens with a memory verse. Then the chapter teaches through a few passages, often by staying with a woman in Scripture: Mary at her brother's tomb, the woman who reached for the hem, the woman at the well. A short sidebar called Digging Deeper is there for the woman who wants to go further.
  • Reflect. Five reflection questions, each meant to be answered in a few honest sentences. Some begin "In your journal," and some ask you to share with your group.
  • Respond. Written exercises with space for your answers, an Integration Bridge that gives you one small thing to try "this week" when a specific moment comes, and a closing prayer written in full.

The book gives one chapter to each week and sets no daily schedule, except in Week 3, where it asks for 15 to 20 minutes a day for a seven-day prayer. A Bible study for beginners does not need to be longer than that.

A first session for beginners: Mary at the tomb

Week 1 of the study is about the wound you stopped naming, and one of its passages is John 11. Lazarus has died, and his sister Mary comes to Jesus. It is a good first passage for a hurting heart because nobody in it is pretending. Mary did not tidy her grief before she brought it to Jesus.

Mary did not tidy her grief before she brought it to Jesus.

Here are the four verses at the center of the scene:

"Then when Mary was come where Jesus was, and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying unto him, Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died. When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping which came with her, he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled, And said, Where have ye laid him? They said unto him, Lord, come and see. Jesus wept." (John 11:32-35, KJV)

What you need: a Bible, a notebook and a pen. How long: about twenty minutes. If you only have ten, do steps 1 to 4 and stop there.

  1. Write the date and one line. At the top of the page, write "What I'm bringing today:" and finish it with a word. Grief. My marriage. I don't know. Any of those will do.
  2. Read the whole story once. Read John 11:17-35 at your normal pace, just to know what happens. Lazarus has been in the grave four days, and Martha meets Jesus on the road first.
  3. Read verses 32 to 35 again, slowly. Aloud if you can.
  4. Write down only what the text says. Four or five plain lines: where Mary goes, what she does, what she says, what Jesus asks, what He does. Feelings can wait for the next steps.
  5. Look back at verse 21. Martha said the same sentence on the road: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." (John 11:21, KJV) Mary says it at His feet. With Martha, Jesus talks about the resurrection. With Mary, He asks one question and weeps. Underline the phrase in verses 32 to 35 that stopped you.
  6. Answer one question in your notebook. The book asks it right after this passage: "What wound have you been keeping at a distance from God because you thought you needed to process it more before you brought it to Him?" Three or four honest sentences are enough.
  7. Write your own sentence to Him. Begin with Mary's first word, "Lord," and say the true thing as plainly as she did. Jesus did not correct her for saying hers.
  8. Choose one small thing for this week. This is the study's Integration Bridge for Week 1: when someone asks how you are and you feel the pull to say "I'm good, just busy, trusting God," pause for two seconds and admit the truth to yourself, even silently.
  9. Close in prayer. Use your own words, or borrow a line from the book's closing prayer for this week: "You wept at a tomb knowing resurrection was coming. Weep with me now."

That is one sitting from the first week. Healing Bible Study for Women gives you six weeks of them: naming the wound you stopped naming, finding the lies that took root while you were hurting, the God who heals what medicine can't, forgiveness and what Scripture actually requires, rebuilding your identity, boundaries and spiritual rhythms with Nehemiah, and walking out whole with the woman who left her water jar. Each week has its memory verse, five reflection questions, written exercises and a closing prayer, and the paperback leaves lined space for your answers. A short conclusion helps you look back over all six weeks.

What you might notice

You may cry. Tears in a first session do not mean you did it wrong, and the passage itself is full of weeping. You may feel a little less alone with the hard thing.

You may also notice nothing at all. The words can look flat, and step 6 can stay unanswered. That is an honest result, and it needs no fixing. Write "nothing came today" and come back to the same four verses tomorrow.

A Bible study is no promise that the hurt will lift, and a hurt that stays says nothing about the size of your faith. If the pain is deep, or has gone on a long time, it can also deserve the help of a pastor, a counselor or a doctor. The book says it plainly: "Some wounds need more than a Bible study can give."

When to use it: alone, with a friend, or in a small group

  • Alone. Early, before the phone, or at night once the house is quiet. Leave the notebook where you will see it tomorrow.
  • With a friend. Read the passage aloud together, do steps 4 to 7 on your own, then share only what you want to. The book says naming is "more powerful when it's spoken aloud to someone who receives it well."
  • In a small group. The book's note for leaders: use the reflection questions as a discussion guide, one chapter a week, go slowly, keep what is shared in the room, and let women pass when a question is too much.

If step 7 brought up an old hurt that needs more than one sentence, how to lament with a written prayer from Lamentations 3 comes from the same first week. If you are waiting on a body to heal, these healing scriptures for the woman tired of asking come from Week 3. And on days a whole study feels like too much, these prayer journal ideas for when you don't know what to say give you a first line.

Questions women ask about Bible study for women

Where should a beginner start a Bible study? With one short passage and a notebook, not a whole book of the Bible. A scene like John 11:32-35 works well: read it twice, write down what it says, and answer one honest question.

How long should I study the Bible each day? About twenty minutes is enough for the session above, and ten will do if you stop after step 4. The study it comes from takes one chapter a week and, in Week 3, asks for 15 to 20 minutes a day.

Should I do a Bible study alone or in a group? Either works. Alone, you go at your own pace. With a friend or a small group, the reflection questions become a conversation, as long as everyone is free to pass.

The Bible on the nightstand is still there. Tonight it can lie open at four verses, with one honest line under them in your handwriting.

This study comes from Healing Bible Study for Women by Hannah Grace. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.

author: hannah-grace
title: Prayer Journal Prompts for When Life Is Heavy
dek: Prayer journal prompts for heavy seasons: seven pages from a guided journal, each with its KJV verse, and a worry-to-prayer practice for today.
seo_title: Prayer Journal Prompts for When Life Is Heavy
seo_description: Prayer journal prompts for hard times: seven KJV pages for grief, fear, waiting and shame, plus a worry, request and thanks practice for today.
pull_quote: A heavy prayer does not have to sound settled to be a prayer.
body_html:
It is 3 a.m. and the house is dark. The worry that sat with you all day has followed you to bed, and the prayer you try to say keeps falling apart halfway through. You know God is listening. You just can't find the words.

These prayer journal prompts are for nights like that, and for the mornings after. They come from Part Two of Daily Prayer Journal for Women, a section called When Life Is Heavy, which opens with this line: "Some seasons, prayer feels less like a conversation and more like holding on." Below are seven prompts from its pages, each with the verse it rests on, and one complete practice you can do today with a pen and any sheet of paper.

What to pray when life is hard

A prompt hands you the first half of a sentence, and you only have to finish it. The book puts it simply: "You don't have to tidy them up first. Bring them as they are."

Every week of Part Two opens with a King James verse, a short reflection, a prayer to begin and a practice drawn from that verse. Then each daily entry asks the same four things:

  • "What feels heavy today"
  • "What I'm placing in Your hands"
  • "A promise I'm holding onto"
  • "Thank You, even today, for"

Those four lines are a prompt in themselves. On a hard day, filling only the first one is still a prayer.

Seven prayer journal prompts for hard days

Each comes from a different page of Part Two. Copy the words in quotation marks and write underneath.

  • Name the heaviest thing (Part Two opener). Before the first week begins, there is one page with one prompt: "What feels heaviest right now, and what I'm asking God to do."
  • Yet I remember (Week 15, When Your Heart Is Broken). The verse is "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." (Psalm 34:18, KJV) The week's lament has five steps, and the middle one turns the prayer: "Yet I remember: a time He was near, or a promise." If the grief is old and has never had words, how to lament a wound you stopped naming walks through a longer written lament.
  • Soar, run, or walk? (Week 16, When You Are Waiting). Isaiah names three paces: "they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint." (Isaiah 40:31, KJV) Circle the one that is true this week and finish the line "The strength I need for this pace." The book adds: "All three count."
  • The fear I am naming (Week 17, When You Are Afraid). Isaiah 41:10 holds five promises, beginning "Fear thou not; for I am with thee" (KJV). Pick the one you need most. Write "The fear I am naming," then "What this promise says to that fear."
  • Talk to your soul (Week 20, When Life Disappoints You). The psalmist asks himself a question: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God" (Psalm 42:11, KJV). Write the first half as a heading and let your soul answer honestly. Then write "Hope thou in God" and reply the way a kind friend would.
  • Two voices (Week 23, When Shame Speaks). Draw a line down the middle of the page. On the left, under "What shame says," write its exact words. On the right, under "What God says," answer each line with "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1, KJV).
  • Tonight I hand You (Week 25, When You Cannot Rest). Before you sleep, list what you can't fix tonight, and check each one as you hand it to God. The page closes with "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep" (Psalm 4:8, KJV).

For the gentler starting points from the first part of the same journal, see prayer journal ideas for when you don't know what to say.

Prayer prompts for hard times are not a test

Picture a woman I'll call Dana. She is a composite, drawn from what many women describe. Every prayer she starts turns into the same worry written a new way, and she believes a good prayer should sound settled. Week 14 reads Paul's words, written from prison, and notes: "He didn't promise the problem would disappear. He promised a peace that would stand guard over your heart and mind." A heavy prayer does not have to sound settled to be a prayer.

A heavy prayer does not have to sound settled to be a prayer.

A practice for today: worry, request, thanks

This is the Week 14 practice, from When You Are Anxious, moved onto plain paper. It rests on this verse:

"Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus." (Philippians 4:6-7, KJV)

"Be careful for nothing" is the old English way of saying don't be anxious about anything. The book's instruction is short: "turn each worry into a request, then add a thank-you. One row per worry." It sets no length of time. Ten to fifteen minutes is enough.

  1. Read the verse slowly, once, out loud if you can.
  2. Draw three columns and label them "My worry," "What I ask instead" and "Thank You for."
  3. Write one worry in the first column, as plainly as you would say it to a friend: the test result, the bill.
  4. Turn it into a request in the second column. Ask for something specific, such as courage for the conversation or sleep tonight.
  5. Add one thank-you in the third column. It doesn't have to match the worry. Something small counts.
  6. Repeat, one row per worry, until the worries you came with are on the page or you are ready to stop.
  7. Close with the week's prayer: "Lord, You see every worry I'm carrying. I'm turning them into prayers right now. Guard my heart and mind with Your peace."

In Daily Prayer Journal for Women, this page is already drawn, and it is one of thirteen weeks in Part Two, Weeks 14 to 26, each with its own verse, reflection, prayer and practice. Six daily entries a week carry the four heavy-day lines, printed and waiting for a date, and a Day 7 page asks two questions written for that week's verse, such as "Which worry did I turn into a prayer this week? What happened in me afterward?" Before the first week, a page called When It Feels Heavy sets out how to carry the tender pages: go at your own pace, know when to stop, and close the page gently.

What you might notice

You might notice the first column fills quickly and the second one slowly. Asking can be harder than worrying. You might also notice nothing. The worry may still be there when you put the pen down. That is an honest result, and it says nothing about whether you were heard.

Tears are possible too, sometimes on the thank-you column of all places. Let them come. The journal's advice after a heavy page is to do something with your body: "Stand up, stretch, drink a glass of water, or step outside for a minute. Then say one sentence of thanks, even a small one." If the heaviness doesn't lift by the end of the day, set the page aside and talk to someone you trust. A heavy season can also deserve a pastor, a counselor or a doctor, and reaching for one is not a failure of prayer. If you are thinking about harming yourself, call or text 988 in the United States, or your local emergency number.

When to use it

  • When worry wakes you at night. One row is enough.
  • Before a hard appointment or phone call. In the parked car, with the engine off.
  • At the end of a long week. Read back over your rows: "Prayers answered, and prayers I'm still waiting on."

Questions women ask about prayer journal prompts

What should I write in a prayer journal when life is hard? Start with one line: "What feels heavy today." Then, if you can, "What I'm placing in Your hands," "A promise I'm holding onto" and "Thank You, even today, for." Filling only the first line is still a prayer.

What if I'm too tired or sad to write much? Write as much or as little as you can, and stop whenever you need to. The journal calls every practice "an invitation, not an assignment." A single row of worry, request and thanks is a full entry.

Is it okay to write angry or doubtful prayers? The psalmist asked his own soul why it was cast down, and the book calls that "a question, not a scolding." Part Two gives whole weeks to anger, disappointment and shame. Write them honestly, then add one line that begins "Yet I remember."

The house will be dark again some night. The page beside the bed will already have a first line on it.

These prompts come from Daily Prayer Journal for Women by Hannah Grace. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.

title: Scripture Writing for Beginners: How to Write, Reflect On and Remember a Verse
dek: Scripture writing for beginners: what it is, three simple ways to reflect on a verse, and a fifteen-minute first session with Psalm 103:8 (KJV).
seo_title: Scripture Writing for Beginners: How to Start (KJV)
seo_description: Scripture writing for beginners: how to write, reflect on and remember a verse, three reflection pages and a first session with Psalm 103:8.
pull_quote: One verse, one pen and one honest response are enough to count.
body_html:
The notebook has been on your nightstand for three weeks. You saw photos of other women's pages, the neat handwriting and the verse in soft ink, and you thought you could do that. Then you opened it and did not know which verse to choose, or what you were supposed to write after you copied it.

This is scripture writing for beginners, starting from the first page. You copy one short Bible verse by hand, word for word, and then you spend a few minutes with it on paper. That second part is where most of us get stuck, so here are three simple ways to do it and one full first session you can try tonight.

What is scripture writing?

Scripture writing is copying a passage of the Bible by hand, slowly, in the exact words of the translation you are using. It is not a commentary study, and it is not art journaling, though you can add color later if you like. One verse, one pen and one honest response are enough to count.

One verse, one pen and one honest response are enough to count.

The simplest shape I know comes from my Scripture Journal for Women, where every passage gets two pages. On the first you write it out. On the second you reflect, and the reflection pages take turns among three kinds: Look Closer, Make It Personal and Hide It in My Heart. A beginner does not need all three at once. Pick one reflection for each verse, and let the next verse take the next one.

Every verse below is from the King James Version. Its words are old, and copying them exactly is part of the work.

Scripture writing for beginners: three ways to reflect

Here is what each reflection page asks, with passages from the first part of the journal, Who God Is, as examples.

Look Closer. This page is for noticing. You write the word or phrase that stopped you, then what it shows you about God. It also asks you to pray the verse back in your own words and to name one way to live it today. In the journal, Psalm 90:2 gets this page: "Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God." (Psalm 90:2, KJV) Its question asks what feels urgent in your life this week that looks different next to an everlasting God.

Make It Personal. This page is for translating. You rewrite the passage the way you would say it to a friend, then write where you need it right now, and finish with a short prayer. Isaiah 40:28 gets this page, and it suits a long KJV sentence well: "Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding." (Isaiah 40:28, KJV) The question beside it: where have I been assuming God is as tired of my struggles as I am?

Hide It in My Heart. This page is for remembering. You cover the verse and write it again from memory. The page says it plainly: peek if you need to, memory grows by trying. Then it asks who might need to hear this verse, and leaves a line that begins Lord, help me. The first session below uses this page.

How to do scripture writing: your first session

What you need: a King James Bible or the verse printed out, a pen, and any lined notebook. How long: about fifteen minutes. If you only have five, do steps 1 to 3 and stop. The reflection can wait.

The verse is Psalm 103:8. It is thirteen words long, a good size for a first time: "The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy." (Psalm 103:8, KJV)

  1. Read the verse aloud once. Slowly, all the way to the last word, before you pick up the pen.
  2. Copy it word for word. Keep LORD in capitals and keep "plenteous." Do not tidy the old words into new ones.
  3. Check your copy against the Bible. Go word by word with your finger. If you dropped an "and," fix it. This is where the small words start to show up.
  4. Cover both and write it again from memory. Peek if you need to. Memory grows by trying.
  5. Answer one question in three or four sentences. The journal asks of this verse: how does a God who is slow to anger change the way I come to Him after I fail?
  6. Write one name. Under "Who might need to hear this?" put the first person who comes to mind. You do not have to send it to anyone.
  7. Close with one line that begins "Lord, help me." Finish it honestly, then shut the notebook.

In Scripture Journal for Women, Psalm 103:8 is passage 5 of 96. It is printed at the top of a lined page, so there is nothing to look up, and the page after it is a Hide It in My Heart reflection with that question already written. All 96 KJV passages work the same way, each with its own question and the three reflection pages taking turns. What the journal adds is the rest of the method: twelve parts, each with a short introduction and a checklist of its eight passages; one creative practice in every part, starting with a map of God's name in Exodus 34:6; a Looking Back page at the end of each part; and a tracker with 96 squares to shade. A plain notebook will hold this first session just as well.

What you might notice

You might notice a word you have read past before. "Plenteous" is an unusual word to write by hand, and your pen may slow down on it. You might notice that step 4 is harder than you expected. Or you might notice nothing at all.

Nothing is an honest result. The verse is on the page in your handwriting either way, and the next session does not depend on how this one felt.

Some verses touch tender places. If a question opens something painful, you can copy the verse and leave the rest for another day. If the heaviness does not lift by the end of the day, set the page aside and talk to someone you trust: a friend, your pastor or a counselor.

When to use this first session

  • The first time you try scripture writing. Use Psalm 103:8 and the seven steps as written.
  • Before you choose a plan. A session or two shows you what pace you can keep: one verse a day, a few each week, or one every Sunday afternoon.
  • After a long gap. If weeks have gone by, start again with one short verse and steps 1 to 3. Nothing resets.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Choosing a plan with dates and falling behind. The journal has no dates on purpose, so you can't fall behind. If you miss a day, skip it and keep going.
  • Thinking a session without reflection does not count. If you only have five minutes, just write the verse.
  • Modernizing the words. Copy word for word, old verb endings included. Changing "fainteth" to "faints" turns copying into paraphrase, and Make It Personal is the page for your own words.
  • Refusing to peek. Writing from memory is not a test. Peek if you need to.
  • Pushing through a heavy page. Every question is an invitation, not an assignment. You can skip it, change it or stop halfway.

Where to go after your first session

Once a few sessions feel natural, a plan saves you from choosing the next verse. The December scripture writing plan takes eight KJV passages on peace across four weeks, two a week, with rest days. The 2027 scripture writing plan sets twelve themes across the year, one a month. And if your "Lord, help me" line keeps growing into a page, these prayer journal ideas for when you don't know what to say show how to begin a prayer journal.

Questions women ask about scripture writing for beginners

What is scripture writing? It is copying a Bible passage by hand, word for word, in the translation you are using, and then responding to it on paper. In this method, every verse gets a written copy and one reflection: Look Closer, Make It Personal or Hide It in My Heart.

How long should a beginner spend on scripture writing? About fifteen minutes for the full first session above. On a five-minute day, read the verse, copy it and check it. The reflection can wait.

Do I have to memorize the verse? No. Writing from memory is one of the three reflection pages, not a requirement for every verse. When you do try it, peek if you need to, because memory grows by trying.

The notebook on the nightstand needs only one verse to stop being blank. Psalm 103:8 is thirteen words.

This method comes from Scripture Journal for Women by Hannah Grace. Scripture quotations are from the King James Version.
